lessonTitle: The Navier-Stokes Equations and the No-Slip Condition

blocks.text: The oil film in a hydraulic valve spool, the blood in an artery and the air over a car roof all obey the same set of equations: Newton's second law written for a small parcel of fluid. Those equations, the Navier-Stokes equations, look intimidating, but for the straight, steady flows met in engineering most terms vanish and what remains is a pressure-viscous balance you can solve with pen and paper.

blocks.markdown: The Navier-Stokes equations express Newton's second law, **mass times acceleration equals the sum of forces**, for a fluid element of an incompressible Newtonian fluid of constant density $\rho$ and constant viscosity $\mu$. Together with the continuity equation $\nabla\cdot\mathbf V=0$ they govern the velocity $\mathbf V(x,y,z,t)$ and pressure $p$. In vector form, per unit volume (units N/m$^3$):

blocks.title: The four groups of terms
blocks.text:
Left side: the **inertia** (mass times acceleration) terms: $ho\,\partial\mathbf V/\partial t$ is the local (unsteady) acceleration and $ho\,\mathbf V\cdot
abla\mathbf V$ is the convective acceleration, which is non-linear. Right side: $-
abla p$ is the **pressure** force, $\mu
abla^2\mathbf V$ is the **viscous** force from the stress gradients, and $ho\mathbf g$ is the **body force** (gravity). Each has units of force per unit volume.

blocks.markdown: In Cartesian coordinates the $x$-component is $\rho\left(\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t}+u\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}+v\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}+w\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z}\right)=-\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x}+\mu\left(\dfrac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}+\dfrac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2}+\dfrac{\partial^2u}{\partial z^2}\right)+\rho g_x$, with similar $y$ and $z$ equations. The ratio of the size of the convective inertia term, of order $\rho U^2/L$, to the viscous term, of order $\mu U/L^2$, is $\rho UL/\mu=Re$, the Reynolds number: at low $Re$ viscous forces dominate and at high $Re$ inertia dominates.

blocks.caption: Identification of the terms in the incompressible Navier-Stokes equation

blocks.markdown: **Simplification for unidirectional flow.** Consider steady, incompressible, fully developed flow between two parallel plates, with the velocity along $x$ only and depending only on $y$: $\mathbf V=(u(y),0,0)$. Continuity is satisfied automatically since $\partial u/\partial x=0$. Every convective term vanishes because $v=w=0$ and $\partial u/\partial x=0$, the unsteady term vanishes because the flow is steady, and the $x$-derivatives of $u$ in the viscous term vanish. The $y$-momentum equation gives $\partial p/\partial y=-\rho g$, so $p$ varies hydrostatically across the gap; absorbing gravity into a modified pressure, the $x$-equation reduces to the ODE below.

blocks.caption: Reduced x-momentum equation for steady fully developed flow, u = u(y)

blocks.title: No-slip boundary condition
blocks.text: A viscous fluid in contact with a solid surface moves with the same velocity as the surface (tangential component), so $u_{fluid}=u_{wall}$ at the wall: zero for a fixed wall, $U$ for a wall moving at $U$. The normal component of the fluid velocity also matches the wall for an impermeable surface. These conditions supply the constants of integration.

blocks.title: Plane Poiseuille flow between fixed plates
blocks.prompt: Derive the velocity profile for steady laminar flow between two fixed parallel plates at y = 0 and y = h driven by a constant pressure gradient dp/dx = -G, where G > 0. Then evaluate for oil (typical density 900 kg/m^3, viscosity 0.10 Pa s), h = 4.0 mm and G = 400 Pa/m: maximum velocity, flow rate per unit width, wall shear and the Reynolds number.

steps.text: Start from the reduced momentum equation with dp/dx = -G and integrate twice.
Apply no-slip at the lower wall, u(0) = 0, giving C2 = 0, and at the upper wall u(h) = 0, giving C1 = G h/(2 mu).
The maximum is at the centre y = h/2; integrate u over the gap for the flow rate per unit width.
Wall shear stress from tau_w = mu du/dy at y = 0, which equals G h/2.
Mean velocity is q/h = 0.00533 m/s, so the Reynolds number based on the gap h is small, confirming that viscous forces dominate.

blocks.title: Using no-slip in Couette flow
blocks.prompt: Oil of typical viscosity 0.080 Pa s fills a gap h = 3.0 mm between a fixed lower plate and an upper plate moving at U = 0.60 m/s, with no pressure gradient. Use the reduced Navier-Stokes equation and the no-slip conditions to find the velocity profile and the shear stress.

steps.text: With dp/dx = 0 the reduced equation is mu u'' = 0; integrating twice gives a linear profile with two constants.
Fixed lower plate: no-slip gives u(0) = 0 so C2 = 0. Moving upper plate: no-slip gives u(h) = U so C1 = U/h = 0.60/0.0030 = 200 per second.
Shear stress is viscosity times the constant velocity gradient and is the same at both plates.

blocks.answer: u = 200 y (m/s, y in m); the shear stress is 16.0 Pa everywhere in the gap.

items: Write the full Navier-Stokes $x$-component and the continuity equation.
Cross out every term that is zero by assumption (steady, unidirectional, fully developed, no variation in $x$ or $z$).
Integrate the remaining ODE and keep the integration constants.
Apply no-slip on each wall (and symmetry or zero shear where appropriate).
Check the Reynolds number: the laminar solution is valid only if the flow stays laminar.

blocks.title: Why exact solutions exist
blocks.text: The convective acceleration is the only non-linear term. In unidirectional flow it vanishes identically, so the Navier-Stokes equation becomes linear and can be integrated exactly. In general flows the non-linearity makes closed-form solutions rare, which is why numerical methods are used.

blocks.title: Pressure and gravity
blocks.text: In the vertical direction the pressure is hydrostatic. Combine $p$ and gravity into a piezometric pressure $p^*=p+\rho gz$ when gravity matters, and remember that only the pressure gradient along the flow drives it. Also a no-slip condition applies to the tangential velocity relative to the wall; it fails for rarefied gases at very small scales.

points:
The incompressible Navier-Stokes equation is inertia $=$ pressure $+$ viscous $+$ body force; the terms are $ho\,\partial\mathbf V/\partial t+ho\,\mathbf V\cdot
abla\mathbf V=-
abla p+\mu
abla^2\mathbf V+ho\mathbf g$.
For steady unidirectional flow $u=u(y)$ the equation reduces to $\mu\,d^2u/dy^2=dp/dx$.
The no-slip condition sets the fluid velocity equal to the wall velocity and provides the boundary conditions.
Plane Poiseuille flow gives $u=Gy(h-y)/(2\mu)$ with $q=Gh^3/(12\mu)$ and $\tau_w=Gh/2$.

questions.stem: In the incompressible Navier-Stokes equation, which term represents the viscous force per unit volume?

options.text: rho times the velocity dotted with the gradient of velocity
mu times the Laplacian of the velocity

questions.correctOptionText: mu times the Laplacian of the velocity

distractorRationale.a: This is the convective acceleration (inertia) term.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the viscous force comes from the divergence of the viscous stress, giving mu del-squared V.
distractorRationale.d: This is the pressure force, minus the pressure gradient.

questions.explanation: The viscous stress tensor for a Newtonian fluid with constant viscosity has divergence $\mu\nabla^2\mathbf V$ for incompressible flow, so this term is the net viscous force per unit volume. The others are the pressure, inertia and body force terms.

questions.stem: Which term in the Navier-Stokes equation is non-linear in the velocity and so makes general solutions difficult?

options.text: The viscous term, mu del-squared V
The convective acceleration, rho (V . grad) V

questions.correctOptionText: The convective acceleration, rho (V . grad) V

distractorRationale.a: This term does not depend on V at all.
distractorRationale.b: This term is linear in V.
distractorRationale.c: This term is linear in p (and the pressure is an independent unknown).
distractorRationale.d: Correct: it contains products of velocity components and their derivatives.

questions.explanation: The convective acceleration $\rho\,\mathbf V\cdot\nabla\mathbf V$ multiplies the velocity by its own gradient, a quadratic quantity in $\mathbf V$. All the other terms are linear in the unknowns.

questions.stem: Steady, incompressible flow between two fixed parallel plates is fully developed with velocity u(y) only. Which equation results from the x-momentum equation (G = -dp/dx > 0)?

distractorRationale.a: This applies when there is no pressure gradient (Couette flow).
distractorRationale.b: Correct: all inertia terms vanish and a pressure gradient balances viscous stress.
distractorRationale.c: Convective terms vanish because du/dx = 0 in fully developed flow.
distractorRationale.d: Gravity acts in the y direction in this configuration and is balanced by hydrostatic pressure, not by shear.

questions.explanation: With $v=w=0$, $\partial u/\partial x=0$ and steady flow, the inertia terms drop out, leaving $0=-dp/dx+\mu\,d^2u/dy^2$, that is $\mu\,u''=-G$.

questions.stem: Oil (viscosity 0.020 Pa s) flows steadily between two fixed horizontal plates 2.0 mm apart under a pressure gradient of magnitude 1500 Pa/m. Using the laminar solution u = G y (h - y)/(2 mu), find the maximum velocity (at the mid-plane) in m/s.

A viscous liquid of viscosity 0.040 Pa s flows between two fixed parallel plates separated by 5.0 mm, driven by a pressure gradient of magnitude 200 Pa/m. Using q = G h^3/(12 mu), find the volume flow rate per metre of plate width in m^3/s per metre (m^2/s).
questions.explanation: q = G h^3/(12 mu) = 200 x (0.005)^3/(12 x 0.040) = 5.208e-05 m^2/s, i.e. 52.1 cm^3/s for each metre of plate width.

questions.stem: The no-slip condition means that a viscous fluid in contact with a solid wall has the same tangential velocity as the wall, even if the wall itself is moving.
questions.explanation: No-slip equates the fluid's velocity at the surface with that of the wall: zero for a stationary wall and $U$ for a wall moving at $U$. This is why the moving plate in Couette flow drags the adjacent fluid at speed $U$.

questions.stem: Fluid is confined between a stationary lower plate at y = 0 and an upper plate at y = h moving in the x direction at speed U. Which boundary conditions apply?

distractorRationale.a: Zero shear stress at a wall is not a no-slip condition; it holds on a free surface or plane of symmetry.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the fluid adheres to each plate.
distractorRationale.c: The fluid at each wall matches the wall velocity, not the average.
distractorRationale.d: This swaps the plates, so the lower plate would be moving.

questions.explanation: No-slip says that the fluid velocity equals the wall velocity at each wall: $u(0)=0$ at the fixed plate and $u(h)=U$ at the moving plate. These are the conditions that fix the two integration constants.

questions.stem: Water (typical density 998 kg/m^3, viscosity 1.0e-3 Pa s) moves at a characteristic speed of 0.020 m/s through a channel with a characteristic length of 0.050 m. Estimate the ratio of the convective inertia term to the viscous term in the Navier-Stokes equation, i.e. the Reynolds number (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: The inertia term is of order rho U^2/L and the viscous term is of order mu U/L^2, so their ratio is rho U L/mu = 998 x 0.020 x 0.050/1.0e-3 = 998. Inertia is therefore comparable to or larger than the viscous forces.

questions.stem: For steady, incompressible, fully developed flow between two fixed horizontal parallel plates (velocity u(y) in the x direction only), show step by step how the x-momentum Navier-Stokes equation reduces to mu d2u/dy2 = dp/dx. State clearly which terms vanish and why, and describe what the y-momentum equation tells you about the pressure.
markingGuide: Writes the x-momentum equation with all terms: local, convective, pressure, viscous and body force
Unsteady term zero because the flow is steady
Convective terms zero: v = w = 0 and du/dx = 0 from fully developed flow/continuity
Viscous terms d2u/dx2 and d2u/dz2 zero because u depends only on y
Gravity has no x-component for horizontal plates
y-momentum gives dp/dy = -rho g, so pressure is hydrostatic across the gap and dp/dx is the same at all y
questions.explanation: Each assumption removes specific terms: steadiness removes $\partial u/\partial t$, unidirectional fully developed flow removes all convective terms and the $x$ and $z$ viscous derivatives, and horizontal plates mean gravity does not act along $x$. What remains is $\mu u''=dp/dx$, with $p$ hydrostatic in $y$.

questions.stem: Explain the physical meaning of the no-slip boundary condition and use it to determine the constants for plane Poiseuille flow between fixed plates at y = 0 and y = h, starting from u = -G y^2/(2 mu) + C1 y + C2. Hence obtain the wall shear stress and evaluate it for h = 6.0 mm and G = 250 Pa/m.
markingGuide: No-slip: fluid adjacent to a solid has the same tangential velocity as the wall (molecular adhesion and momentum exchange at the surface)
Upper wall u(h) = 0 gives C1 = G h/(2 mu)
tau_w = mu du/dy at y = 0 = G h/2
Numerical value G h/2 = 250 x 0.006/2 = 0.75 Pa
questions.explanation: No-slip fixes both constants: $u(0)=0$ gives $C_2=0$ and $u(h)=0$ gives $C_1=Gh/(2\mu)$, so $u=Gy(h-y)/(2\mu)$. The wall shear stress $\mu\,du/dy|_0=Gh/2$ equals the pressure force on the fluid per unit wall area, giving 0.75 Pa for the stated values.
